experiment_name: Meno-J Experiment 7: v4 Architecture Upgrade and Ablation
research_question: Why might conformal prediction fail to maintain stable coverage across different physiological signal segments?

stage_4_hypotheses.hypothesis: Inter-subject heterogeneity in autonomic regulation causes non-exchangeable residuals across segments, violating conformal prediction's exchangeability assumption.
stage_4_hypotheses.proposed_mechanism: Individual-specific heart rate variability patterns and baroreflex sensitivity create segment-wise residual distributions that differ systematically between subjects, making calibration on pooled data invalid for new subjects.
stage_4_hypotheses.core_assumption: Physiological control parameters (e.g., sympathetic/parasympathetic balance) vary sufficiently across individuals to induce distributional shifts in prediction residuals that are not captured by observed covariates.
stage_4_hypotheses.knowledge_gap_addressed: Lack of quantitative characterization of how inter-individual autonomic differences map to conformal prediction coverage instability in physiological time series.

stage_4_hypotheses.hypothesis: Time-varying sensor impedance and motion artifacts induce segment-dependent noise distributions that break the identical distribution assumption of conformal prediction.
stage_4_hypotheses.proposed_mechanism: Electrode-skin interface impedance drifts and movement artifacts create heteroscedastic, non-stationary noise processes whose statistical properties change across recording segments, causing prediction intervals calibrated on clean segments to undercover on noisy ones.
stage_4_hypotheses.core_assumption: Sensor noise characteristics are not stationary across segments and correlate with physiological state (e.g., movement during stress), violating the i.i.d. assumption for calibration residuals.
stage_4_hypotheses.knowledge_gap_addressed: Insufficient understanding of how real-world wearable sensor degradation and artifact patterns specifically degrade conformal coverage guarantees across signal segments.

stage_4_hypotheses.hypothesis: Transitions between discrete physiological states (e.g., sleep stages, arousal levels) create abrupt distributional shifts in residuals that conformal prediction cannot adapt to without state-aware calibration.
stage_4_hypotheses.proposed_mechanism: Autonomic nervous system state transitions produce step-changes in signal dynamics (e.g., heart rate complexity, respiratory sinus arrhythmia) that alter residual distributions faster than sliding-window recalibration can track.
stage_4_hypotheses.core_assumption: Physiological state changes occur at timescales shorter than the conformal calibration window, and state labels are unavailable or inaccurate for stratification.
stage_4_hypotheses.knowledge_gap_addressed: Unknown relationship between autonomic state transition dynamics and the minimum calibration window size needed for stable conformal coverage in physiological signals.

stage_4_hypotheses.hypothesis: Circadian and ultradian rhythms induce periodic non-stationarity in both signal characteristics and prediction difficulty, causing coverage to oscillate with time-of-day.
stage_4_hypotheses.proposed_mechanism: Endogenous rhythms modulate baseline physiology (e.g., core body temperature, cortisol) and signal-to-noise ratios, creating predictable but unmodeled periodic shifts in residual distributions that fixed calibration sets fail to capture.
stage_4_hypotheses.core_assumption: Rhythmic physiological variations are not fully mediated by observed covariates and have periods comparable to or longer than typical calibration windows.
stage_4_hypotheses.knowledge_gap_addressed: Absence of studies quantifying how circadian/ultradian phase affects conformal prediction coverage stability in continuous physiological monitoring.

stage_4_hypotheses.hypothesis: Inconsistent or noisy ground truth annotations across segments (e.g., sleep stage scoring variability) introduce label noise that corrupts conformal calibration and invalidates coverage guarantees.
stage_4_hypotheses.proposed_mechanism: Inter-rater variability and intra-rater drift in physiological event labeling create segment-dependent label noise distributions, causing the conformity scores to reflect annotation artifacts rather than true prediction uncertainty.
stage_4_hypotheses.core_assumption: Label noise is heteroscedastic across segments and correlates with signal characteristics (e.g., noisier segments receive less reliable annotations), violating the assumption that calibration labels are ground truth.
stage_4_hypotheses.knowledge_gap_addressed: Limited theory on how structured label noise in physiological annotations propagates to conformal prediction coverage failures across data segments.

stage_4_hypotheses.hypothesis: Improper stratification by activity context (e.g., rest vs. exercise) leaves hidden covariate shift between calibration and test segments, causing systematic undercoverage during high-dynamic states.
stage_4_hypotheses.proposed_mechanism: Physical activity fundamentally alters cardiovascular dynamics (e.g., heart rate turbulence, blood pressure variability) and sensor noise, creating distinct residual regimes. Without activity-stratified calibration, intervals calibrated on rest data fail during exercise.
stage_4_hypotheses.core_assumption: Activity context is a strong effect modifier for residual distributions but is either unobserved or not used for stratified conformal prediction.
stage_4_hypotheses.knowledge_gap_addressed: Unknown minimum granularity of activity stratification required for stable conformal coverage across free-living physiological signal segments.

stage_4_hypotheses.hypothesis: Hidden confounding by unmeasured physiological variables (e.g., hydration, medication timing) creates spurious correlations that break exchangeability across segments with different confounder distributions.
stage_4_hypotheses.proposed_mechanism: Unobserved factors simultaneously influence both the physiological signal and the prediction target, inducing segment-wise residual dependencies that conformal prediction's marginal coverage guarantee does not protect against.
stage_4_hypotheses.core_assumption: Key physiological confounders vary systematically across recording sessions/segments and are not captured in the feature set, violating the exchangeability assumption conditional on observed covariates.
stage_4_hypotheses.knowledge_gap_addressed: No established method to detect or quantify hidden confounding effects on conformal prediction coverage in physiological time series without randomized interventions.

stage_4_hypotheses.hypothesis: Variable sampling rates and missing data patterns across segments (e.g., due to Bluetooth dropout) distort residual distributions in ways that conformal prediction's i.i.d. assumption cannot accommodate.
stage_4_hypotheses.proposed_mechanism: Non-random missingness correlated with signal quality (e.g., dropout during motion) creates selection bias in calibration residuals. Imputation or downsampling alters residual distributions differently across segments.
stage_4_hypotheses.core_assumption: Missing data mechanisms are not missing completely at random (MCAR) and vary across segments, inducing distributional shifts in conformity scores that are not accounted for.
stage_4_hypotheses.knowledge_gap_addressed: Lack of conformal prediction theory for irregularly sampled, missing-not-at-random physiological time series with segment-varying observation processes.

stage_4_hypotheses.hypothesis: Finite-sample effects interact with segment length heterogeneity: short segments yield high-variance conformity scores, causing coverage instability that worsens with model complexity.
stage_4_hypotheses.proposed_mechanism: When calibration segments are short relative to model complexity, the empirical quantile of conformity scores becomes a noisy estimator of the true quantile. This noise is amplified for segments with fewer samples, creating segment-length-dependent coverage.
stage_4_hypotheses.core_assumption: Segment lengths vary substantially (e.g., due to event-triggered recording), and the model's effective degrees of freedom are large relative to the shortest segments.
stage_4_hypotheses.knowledge_gap_addressed: No finite-sample coverage bounds for conformal prediction that explicitly account for heterogeneous segment lengths and model complexity in physiological applications.

stage_4_hypotheses.hypothesis: Model misspecification error correlates with physiological signal morphology (e.g., waveform shape), causing residual distributions to shift with morphology changes across segments.
stage_4_hypotheses.proposed_mechanism: The predictive model (e.g., for blood pressure from PPG) has systematic errors that depend on pulse wave morphology. As morphology changes across segments (due to vascular tone, aging, pathology), the residual distribution shifts, breaking coverage.
stage_4_hypotheses.core_assumption: Model error is not independent of signal morphology features that vary across segments, and these morphology features are not included as covariates in the conformal prediction framework.
stage_4_hypotheses.knowledge_gap_addressed: Unknown how morphological variability in physiological waveforms maps to conformal prediction coverage degradation when morphology is not explicitly modeled.

stage_4_2_confounder_rival_builder.rival_prediction: If true physiological ambiguity drives coverage deviation, then segments with low rater agreement but high signal quality will show symmetric coverage errors (both over/under); if label noise drives it, coverage errors will correlate with rater-specific biases (e.g., systematic over-scoring of N3) after controlling for SQI.
stage_4_2_confounder_rival_builder.distinguishing_condition: Using adjudicated labels as ground truth, segments with high initial disagreement (kappa < 0.6) but high SQI show coverage within 2% of nominal when calibrated on adjudicated labels; segments with low SQI show coverage deviation > 8% even with adjudicated labels.
stage_4_2_confounder_rival_builder.confounder_rival_notes: Requires multi-rater annotated data with adjudication. Testable by simulating label noise at known rates vs. selecting genuinely ambiguous segments via physiological features.

possible_confounders: Motion artifacts during exercise corrupting sensor signals (confounded with activity)
Hemodynamic changes (BP, vascular tone) during exercise altering signal morphology independent of autonomic dynamics
Sensor displacement during vigorous activity changing optical path / electrode contact
Sweating altering electrode impedance and PPG baseline
control_variables: Reference-grade signals (arterial line, cuff BP) during controlled exercise protocols
Accelerometer-derived motion artifact metrics (frequency-domain separation)
Skin temperature and sweat rate
Sensor contact force/pressure monitoring (if available)
boring_rival_explanations: Undercoverage during exercise is caused by motion artifacts corrupting the PPG/ECG waveform, not by genuine cardiovascular dynamics changes
Sensor displacement during movement changes the measurement geometry, creating apparent residual shifts that are measurement artifacts
Sweating reduces electrode impedance, changing noise characteristics in a way that mimics physiological non-stationarity
stage_4_2_confounder_rival_builder.rival_prediction: If motion artifacts drive undercoverage, then coverage during exercise will correlate with motion artifact metrics (accelerometer high-frequency power) after controlling for activity intensity (METs); if cardiovascular dynamics drive it, coverage will correlate with hemodynamic markers (pulse transit time, BP variability) after controlling for motion.
stage_4_2_confounder_rival_builder.distinguishing_condition: In a controlled exercise protocol with simultaneous reference BP and wearable PPG, segments matched on METs but differing in motion artifact severity (e.g., cycling vs. running at same METs) show coverage deviation tracking motion metrics (p < 0.01) not METs (p > 0.05).
stage_4_2_confounder_rival_builder.confounder_rival_notes: Critical to separate motion artifact from true physiological non-stationarity. Best tested with reference hemodynamics during controlled activities with different motion profiles at matched intensity.

possible_confounders: Measured covariates that are imperfect proxies for the true confounders (e.g., self-reported medication adherence vs. actual plasma levels)
Time-varying measured covariates not included in the model (e.g., posture, recent food intake)
Selection bias: segments with certain confounder values are more likely to be recorded
Carryover effects from prior segments (e.g., medication half-life, hydration persistence)
control_variables: Objective confounder measures: plasma drug levels, urine specific gravity, salivary caffeine
High-frequency posture/activity monitoring
Segment sequencing and temporal dependency modeling
Sensitivity analysis parameters (Rosenbaum Γ bounds)
boring_rival_explanations: Coverage variation is explained by measured covariates that were omitted from the conformal predictor (e.g., posture, recent caffeine), not by unmeasured confounders
The apparent confounder effect is actually selection bias: segments with extreme confounder values are underrepresented in calibration
Temporal autocorrelation in residuals creates spurious segment-wise coverage variation that mimics confounding
stage_4_2_confounder_rival_builder.rival_prediction: If measured but omitted covariates drive coverage variation, then adding them to the conformal predictor (as stratification or covariates) will eliminate the coverage-confounder correlation; if truly unmeasured confounders drive it, coverage variation will persist even after adjusting for all measured covariates, and sensitivity analysis will require large Γ to explain away.
stage_4_2_confounder_rival_builder.distinguishing_condition: In a dataset with gold-standard confounder measures (plasma drug levels, urine osmolarity), adding these to the conformal framework reduces coverage-confounder correlation to non-significance (p > 0.05) and brings conditional coverage within 2% of nominal across confounder strata.
stage_4_2_confounder_rival_builder.confounder_rival_notes: Requires dataset with measured putative confounders. Testable via sequential addition of confounder proxies to conformal predictor and Rosenbaum sensitivity analysis on residual coverage variation.

possible_confounders: Physiological state changes causing both missingness and signal changes (e.g., arrhythmia causing both dropout and HRV changes)
Device-specific firmware/algorithm differences affecting both sampling and signal processing
Battery voltage drops causing both reduced sampling and sensor performance degradation
Environmental interference (EMI) causing both packet loss and signal corruption
control_variables: Device firmware version and hardware revision
Battery voltage logging
EMI environment monitoring (if feasible)
Simultaneous reference sensor with wired connection
boring_rival_explanations: Missing data is a symptom of physiological events (e.g., arrhythmia, movement) that also change the signal distribution; the missingness mechanism is not the cause
Device firmware updates change both sampling behavior and signal processing, creating apparent missingness effects that are actually software version effects
Low battery reduces both transmission rate and sensor drive current, degrading signal quality independently of missing data pattern
stage_4_2_confounder_rival_builder.rival_prediction: If physiological events drive both missingness and coverage failure, then segments with artificially induced MCAR missingness (simulated dropout) will maintain nominal coverage, while segments with physiologically correlated missingness will not; if missingness mechanism itself drives it, MCAR missingness will also degrade coverage.
stage_4_2_confounder_rival_builder.distinguishing_condition: In a dataset with simultaneous wired reference and wireless wearable, artificially imposing MCAR missingness (random dropout) on the wireless stream at 30% rate yields coverage within 3% of nominal, while the native MNAR missingness at same rate yields coverage deviation > 10%.
stage_4_2_confounder_rival_builder.confounder_rival_notes: Testable by controlled missingness injection experiments on complete datasets with known ground truth. Requires distinguishing missingness mechanism from physiological correlates.

possible_confounders: Segment length correlates with physiological state (e.g., short segments during transitions, long during stable sleep)
Segment length correlates with signal quality (e.g., event-triggered recordings stop when signal degrades)
Model complexity interacts with segment-specific non-stationarity, not just sample size
Calibration segment selection bias: shorter segments may be systematically different
control_variables: Physiological state labels per segment
Signal quality metrics per segment
Explicit modeling of segment-length-dependent quantile estimation error (bootstrap)
Hierarchical/Bayesian conformal methods that pool information across segments
boring_rival_explanations: Short segments have worse coverage because they occur during physiologically unstable periods (transitions, artifacts), not because of finite-sample quantile estimation error
Segment length is a proxy for signal quality: event-triggered recordings capture brief clean epochs; coverage fails due to signal quality, not sample size
The model is misspecified for certain physiological regimes that happen to produce shorter segments; coverage fails due to misspecification, not finite-sample effects
stage_4_2_confounder_rival_builder.rival_prediction: If finite-sample effects drive coverage instability, then coverage variance will scale as √(DoF/n_seg) even when segments are randomly subsampled from a stationary process; if physiological confounding drives it, coverage variance will correlate with state/quality metrics after controlling for n_seg.
stage_4_2_confounder_rival_builder.distinguishing_condition: In a stationary physiological signal (e.g., resting ECG during stable sleep), randomly subsampled segments of varying lengths show coverage variance scaling as √(DoF/n_seg) with no residual correlation with any physiological metric; in real heterogeneous data, this scaling explains < 50% of coverage variance.
stage_4_2_confounder_rival_builder.confounder_rival_notes: Requires separating statistical finite-sample effects from physiological confounding. Best tested by subsampling experiments on known-stationary data vs. real heterogeneous data.

possible_confounders: Covariate shift: morphology distribution changes across segments, but model error is independent of morphology (coverage fails due to covariate shift, not morphology-dependent misspecification)
Unmeasured hemodynamic variables (e.g., vascular resistance, compliance) driving both morphology and target, creating spurious morphology-error correlation
Sensor-specific morphology differences (e.g., wrist vs. finger PPG) confounded with subject groups
Calibration set morphology distribution not representative of deployment distribution (dataset shift)
control_variables: Simultaneous reference waveforms (tonometry, arterial line) for morphology validation
Vascular tone interventions (cold pressor, nitroglycerin, tilt table) to induce controlled morphology shifts
Multi-site PPG recordings to separate sensor-specific from physiological morphology variation
Explicit morphology features as covariates in conformal predictor
boring_rival_explanations: Coverage fails because the test morphology distribution shifts outside the calibration support (covariate shift), not because model error depends on morphology per se
Unmeasured hemodynamic state (e.g., vascular resistance) drives both morphology and BP; model error correlates with morphology only because both correlate with the true driver
Sensor placement differences (wrist vs. finger) create morphology differences that correlate with subject cohorts; coverage fails due to sensor-specific calibration, not morphology-dependent error
stage_4_2_confounder_rival_builder.rival_prediction: If covariate shift drives coverage failure, then importance-weighted conformal prediction (weighting calibration by test morphology density) will restore nominal coverage without adding morphology as a covariate; if morphology-dependent misspecification drives it, importance weighting will fail but morphology-stratified conformal will succeed.
stage_4_2_confounder_rival_builder.distinguishing_condition: In a dataset with induced morphology shifts (vascular interventions), importance-weighted conformal prediction using morphology density ratios achieves coverage within 3% of nominal across all shift magnitudes, while standard conformal shows > 10% deviation; morphology-stratified conformal also works but is not necessary.
stage_4_2_confounder_rival_builder.confounder_rival_notes: Critical distinction: covariate shift vs. concept shift (morphology-dependent error). Testable via vascular interventions that shift morphology while monitoring reference hemodynamics, comparing importance weighting vs. stratification.

stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.effect_size_rationale: Mechanism builder predicts absolute coverage deviation >5% for subjects with high autonomic variability (RMSSD CV >30%) in leave-one-subject-out calibration at nominal 90%.
minimum_data_needed: Multi-subject physiological dataset with ≥50 subjects
Each subject with ≥10 segments of ≥5 min continuous ECG/PPG
Simultaneous reference measurements for prediction target (e.g., cuff BP)
Per-segment HRV metrics (RMSSD, LF/HF ratio) and baroreflex sensitivity estimates
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.testable_prediction: Subjects with autonomic parameter coefficient of variation >30% across the cohort will show mean absolute coverage deviation >5% from nominal 90% in leave-one-subject-out conformal prediction, with a positive correlation between subject-level autonomic distance from calibration pool mean and coverage deviation.
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.failure_condition: If the correlation between subject autonomic parameter distance and coverage deviation is not statistically significant (p>0.05) or the mean absolute coverage deviation for high-variability subjects (top quartile CV) is ≤2%.
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.statistical_test_plan: 1. Compute per-subject autonomic parameters (RMSSD, LF/HF, BRS) for each segment. 2. Perform leave-one-subject-out conformal prediction at nominal 90% coverage. 3. Calculate empirical coverage per subject. 4. Regress absolute coverage deviation on subject-level coefficient of variation of autonomic parameters using linear regression. 5. Test slope ≠ 0 with α=0.05. 6. Bootstrap 95% CI for mean coverage deviation in high-variability vs low-variability subject groups.
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.statistical_testability_notes: Requires sufficient subjects for leave-one-out; if subjects <30, use k-fold subject-wise cross-validation. Control for sensor placement and medication via covariates.

stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.effect_size_rationale: Mechanism builder predicts coverage ≤80% at nominal 90% for top-quartile impedance drift (>20% change) or accelerometer variance segments, versus ≥88% for bottom quartile — a ≥8% absolute difference.
minimum_data_needed: Wearable sensor dataset (PPG/ECG) with simultaneous electrode impedance tracking
Triaxial accelerometer data synchronized with physiological signals
≥100 segments spanning wide range of motion/impedance conditions
Reference signal quality metrics (SNR) per segment
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.testable_prediction: Segments in the top quartile of electrode impedance drift (>20% change) or accelerometer variance will exhibit conformal coverage ≤80% at nominal 90%, while bottom-quartile segments will maintain ≥88% coverage, with a monotonic negative correlation between artifact severity metrics and coverage.
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.failure_condition: If coverage in top-quartile artifact segments is >85% at nominal 90%, or if the correlation between artifact metrics and coverage deviation is not statistically significant (p>0.05) after controlling for physiological state.
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.statistical_test_plan: 1. Quantify per-segment impedance drift (% change) and accelerometer variance. 2. Stratify segments into quartiles by each artifact metric. 3. Compute conformal coverage at nominal 90% per quartile using calibration on bottom-quartile segments. 4. Test coverage difference between top and bottom quartiles with two-proportion z-test (α=0.01). 5. Fit logistic regression of coverage indicator on artifact metrics controlling for HRV. 6. Assess calibration via reliability diagrams per stratum.
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.statistical_testability_notes: Controlled impedance/motion protocols (gel drying, standardized movements) strengthen causal inference. Use reference-grade sensors to isolate artifact effects.

stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.effect_size_rationale: Mechanism builder predicts coverage drops ≥10% below nominal within 2 minutes post-state-transition, with recovery only after calibration window fully contains new-state samples.
minimum_data_needed: Physiological dataset with gold-standard state annotations (e.g., PSG sleep stages)
≥50 state transitions (e.g., NREM→REM, sleep→wake) across subjects
Continuous signals with ≥30 min pre/post-transition per transition
Sliding-window conformal prediction implementation with variable window sizes
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.testable_prediction: Conformal coverage at nominal 90% will drop ≥10% within 2 minutes after verified autonomic state transitions (e.g., N2→REM), with drop magnitude inversely proportional to (window size / state duration) ratio; coverage will recover to within 3% of nominal only after the calibration window contains >80% new-state samples.
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.failure_condition: If coverage drop post-transition is <5% at nominal 90%, or if coverage recovers before the calibration window contains predominantly new-state samples (i.e., recovery time < 0.5 × window size).
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.statistical_test_plan: 1. Align all transitions to t=0. 2. Compute coverage in 30-second bins from -10 to +10 min relative to transition. 3. Fit piecewise linear model to coverage time-course; test slope change at t=0 (α=0.01). 4. Vary calibration window size (1, 5, 15, 30 min) and measure minimum coverage and recovery time. 5. Compare coverage drop across transition types (N2→REM vs N3→wake) with ANOVA. 6. Test interaction between window size and transition type.
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.statistical_testability_notes: Requires high-resolution state labels; use PSG-scored data. Control for movement artifacts during transitions via accelerometer stratification.

stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.effect_size_rationale: Mechanism builder predicts coverage oscillation amplitude ≥5% at nominal 90% across circadian phases, with minimum coverage at circadian trough (~04:00-06:00).
minimum_data_needed: Continuous physiological monitoring ≥48 hours per subject (≥20 subjects)
Circadian phase markers (DLMO, core body temperature rhythm, or validated proxy)
Segments binned into ≥6 circadian phase bins (4-hour width)
Conformal prediction with fixed calibration window shorter than 24h
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.testable_prediction: Conformal coverage at nominal 90% will oscillate with a 24-hour period (cosinor amplitude ≥2.5%, p<0.05), reaching minimum at circadian phases corresponding to peak residual variance (e.g., 04:00-06:00), and phase-stratified calibration will reduce oscillation amplitude by ≥50% compared to fixed calibration.
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.failure_condition: If cosinor analysis yields amplitude <1.5% (p>0.05) or if phase-stratified calibration does not reduce coverage oscillation amplitude by at least 30%.
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.statistical_test_plan: 1. Bin segments by circadian phase relative to DLMO (4-hour bins). 2. Compute coverage per bin at nominal 90%. 3. Fit cosinor model: coverage ~ mesor + amplitude*cos(2πt/24 + phase). 4. Test amplitude >0 with bootstrap CI (α=0.05). 5. Compare fixed-window vs phase-stratified (6 strata) calibration using paired t-test on per-bin coverage deviations. 6. Correlate residual variance with CBT proxy across bins.
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.statistical_testability_notes: Constant routine or forced desynchrony data provide gold-standard circadian phase; in observational data, use DLMO or CBT minimum as phase anchor. Control for activity/sleep via covariates.

stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.effect_size_rationale: Mechanism builder predicts segments with inter-rater kappa <0.7 show coverage deviation ≥8% from nominal, with direction depending on noise asymmetry.
minimum_data_needed: Multi-rater annotated physiological dataset (≥3 raters, ≥100 segments)
Adjudicated consensus labels as ground truth reference
Per-segment signal quality indices (SQI)
Rater identity and experience metadata
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.testable_prediction: Segments with inter-rater agreement (Cohen's kappa) <0.7 will show absolute coverage deviation ≥8% from nominal 90% when calibrated on single-rater labels, but coverage will be within 2% of nominal when calibrated on adjudicated labels; coverage deviation will correlate with rater-specific bias patterns after controlling for SQI.
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.failure_condition: If coverage deviation in low-agreement segments (kappa<0.7) is <4% when using single-rater labels, or if adjudicated-label calibration does not reduce deviation by at least 50%.
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.statistical_test_plan: 1. Compute per-segment inter-rater kappa and SQI. 2. Run conformal prediction at nominal 90% using each single rater's labels and adjudicated labels separately. 3. Compare coverage deviation (|empirical - nominal|) between low-kappa (<0.7) and high-kappa (≥0.7) segments via Mann-Whitney U test. 4. Regress coverage deviation on kappa, SQI, and rater bias indicators. 5. Simulate label noise at known rates (5%, 10%, 20%) and measure coverage degradation slope.
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.statistical_testability_notes: Requires multi-rater data with adjudication (e.g., MASS, Sleep-EDF). Test both symmetric and asymmetric noise simulations.

stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.effect_size_rationale: Mechanism builder predicts undercoverage ≥15% at nominal 90% during vigorous activity (METs>6) when calibrated on mixed/rest data, with overcoverage ≥5% during rest if calibration dominated by exercise.
minimum_data_needed: Free-living dataset with synchronized accelerometer and physiological signals (PPG/ECG)
Activity classification (rest, walk, run, bike) with METs estimates
≥100 segments per activity intensity stratum
Reference target measurements (e.g., cuff BP) during activities
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.testable_prediction: Unstratified conformal prediction calibrated on mixed-activity data will show coverage ≤75% at nominal 90% during vigorous activity (METs>6) and ≥95% during rest; activity-stratified calibration (minimum 4 strata: rest, light, moderate, vigorous) will restore coverage to within 3% of nominal per stratum.
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.failure_condition: If unstratified coverage during vigorous activity is >85% at nominal 90%, or if activity-stratified calibration fails to bring all strata within 5% of nominal coverage.
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.statistical_test_plan: 1. Classify segments by activity type/intensity (METs bins). 2. Compute coverage per stratum using unstratified calibration (all data). 3. Test coverage difference between vigorous and rest strata with two-proportion z-test. 4. Implement activity-stratified conformal prediction (separate calibration per stratum). 5. Compare per-stratum coverage deviations between unstratified and stratified via paired bootstrap. 6. Determine minimum strata granularity by sequentially merging strata until coverage deviation >5% in any stratum.
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.statistical_testability_notes: Control for motion artifacts via reference signals during controlled exercise. Use datasets like PPG-DaLiA, WESAD, or Apple Watch studies.

stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.effect_size_rationale: Mechanism builder predicts coverage deviation correlates with confounder distribution shift (|coverage-nominal|>0.05 when KL divergence>0.5) and medication-on vs off shows ≥10% coverage gap.
minimum_data_needed: Dataset with measured confounders (hydration: urine specific gravity; medication: timestamps/plasma levels; caffeine: salivary assays)
≥30 recording sessions per subject with confounder variation
Physiological signals and prediction targets per session
Measured covariates (age, sex, BMI, activity, time-of-day)
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.testable_prediction: Conformal coverage at nominal 90% will deviate by >5% in sessions where unmeasured confounder distribution (e.g., hydration, medication status) shifts substantially (KL divergence >0.5) relative to calibration sessions; adding gold-standard confounder measures to the conformal predictor will reduce coverage-confounder correlation to non-significance (p>0.05) and bring conditional coverage within 2% of nominal across confounder strata.
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.failure_condition: If coverage deviation does not correlate with confounder shift magnitude (p>0.05), or if adding measured confounder proxies fails to reduce coverage variation across confounder strata by at least 50%.
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.statistical_test_plan: 1. Quantify confounder distribution shift per session relative to calibration pool (KL divergence for continuous, chi-square for categorical). 2. Compute per-session coverage at nominal 90%. 3. Regress absolute coverage deviation on shift magnitude (linear regression, α=0.05). 4. Perform Rosenbaum sensitivity analysis: compute Γ required to explain away coverage-confounder association. 5. Add confounder measures as stratification variables; test conditional coverage per stratum vs nominal (binomial test). 6. Compare marginal vs conditional coverage gap.
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.statistical_testability_notes: Gold-standard confounder measures (plasma drug levels, urine osmolarity) are critical. If unavailable, use sensitivity analysis bounds. Simulate hidden confounding by omitting known confounders.

stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.effect_size_rationale: Mechanism builder predicts segments with MNAR missingness >20% show coverage deviation ≥10% from nominal, while MCAR missingness ≤30% maintains nominal coverage.
minimum_data_needed: Wearable dataset with wireless transmission (Bluetooth) and simultaneous wired reference
Native missing data patterns with mechanism classification (MCAR/MAR/MNAR via Little's test)
Ability to artificially impose controlled missingness (MCAR/MAR/MNAR) at 10-50% rates
Multiple imputation methods (linear, spline, model-based) for comparison
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.testable_prediction: Native MNAR missingness >20% will cause conformal coverage deviation ≥10% from nominal 90%, while artificially imposed MCAR missingness at the same rate will maintain coverage within 3% of nominal; coverage degradation will be specific to missingness mechanism (MNAR >> MAR > MCAR) and imputation method.
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.failure_condition: If MCAR missingness at 30% causes coverage deviation >5%, or if native MNAR missingness at 20% yields coverage deviation <5%, or if mechanism-specific differences are not statistically significant (p>0.01).
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.statistical_test_plan: 1. Classify native missingness mechanism per segment (Little's test). 2. Compute coverage per segment at nominal 90% using standard imputation. 3. Artificially impose MCAR, MAR, MNAR missingness at 10%, 20%, 30%, 40% on complete segments. 4. For each mechanism/rate, compute coverage across 100 imputation replicates. 5. Fit ANOVA: coverage ~ mechanism * rate * imputation_method. 6. Test planned contrasts: MNAR vs MCAR at each rate (α=0.01 with Bonferroni). 7. Evaluate missingness-aware conformal (weighted) vs standard.
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.statistical_testability_notes: Requires simultaneous wired+wireless reference to isolate missingness effects. Test multiple imputation strategies.

stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.effect_size_rationale: Mechanism builder predicts coverage standard deviation across segments scales as √(DoF/n_seg); segments with n_seg/DoF <10 show coverage variance ≥0.02² at nominal 90%.
minimum_data_needed: Physiological dataset with highly heterogeneous segment lengths (30s to 30min)
Known model effective degrees of freedom (DoF) or complexity measure
≥200 segments spanning wide n_seg range
Stationary reference signal for subsampling experiments
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.testable_prediction: Coverage variance across segments will scale linearly with DoF/n_seg (slope ≈1 on log-log scale) when segments are randomly subsampled from a stationary process; in real heterogeneous data, this scaling will explain <50% of coverage variance, with residual variance correlating with physiological state/quality metrics.
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.failure_condition: If coverage variance does not scale with √(DoF/n_seg) in stationary subsampling experiment (p>0.05 for slope=0.5 on log-log), or if finite-sample scaling explains >80% of coverage variance in real heterogeneous data.
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.statistical_test_plan: 1. Subsample stationary reference signal (e.g., stable sleep ECG) to create segments of varying lengths n_seg. 2. Compute coverage per segment at nominal 90% for a model with known DoF. 3. Regress log(coverage variance) on log(DoF/n_seg); test slope = 0.5. 4. In real heterogeneous data, compute coverage variance per segment length bin. 5. Fit mixed model: coverage ~ 1 + (1|segment_length) + physiological_state + signal_quality. 6. Compare variance components. 7. Test hierarchical/Bayesian conformal methods for variance reduction.
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.statistical_testability_notes: Model DoF can be estimated via bootstrap or analytic approximations (e.g., number of parameters, Rademacher complexity). Use event-triggered datasets for natural length heterogeneity.

stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.effect_size_rationale: Mechanism builder predicts coverage deviation >8% when morphology distribution shift (Wasserstein distance) >0.5, and undercoverage ≥15% for segments outside calibration convex hull.
minimum_data_needed: Cuffless BP dataset with simultaneous PPG and reference tonometry/arterial line
Pulse wave morphology features per beat (AIx, PWV, systolic/diastolic peak ratio, entropy)
Controlled morphology shifts via vascular interventions (cold pressor, nitroglycerin, tilt table)
≥50 segments spanning wide morphology distribution
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.testable_prediction: Conformal coverage at nominal 90% will deviate by >8% when test-segment morphology distribution shift (Wasserstein distance on morphology features) exceeds 0.5 relative to calibration; segments with morphology features outside the calibration convex hull will show undercoverage ≥15%; morphology-stratified conformal prediction will restore nominal coverage across all shift magnitudes.
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.failure_condition: If coverage deviation is <4% for Wasserstein distance >0.5, or if morphology-stratified conformal fails to bring coverage within 5% of nominal for out-of-hull segments.
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.statistical_test_plan: 1. Extract morphology features per segment from PPG/tonometry. 2. Compute Wasserstein distance between calibration and test morphology distributions. 3. Bin test segments by shift magnitude. 4. Compute coverage per bin at nominal 90% using standard conformal. 5. Test correlation between shift magnitude and coverage deviation (Spearman, α=0.01). 6. Identify segments outside calibration convex hull (via PCA bounding box). 7. Compare coverage for in-hull vs out-of-hull segments (two-proportion z-test). 8. Implement morphology-stratified conformal (k-means clusters on morphology); test per-stratum coverage.
stage_4_3_statistical_testability_builde.statistical_testability_notes: Vascular interventions (cold pressor, nitroglycerin) induce controlled morphology shifts. Compare importance-weighted conformal vs stratification to distinguish covariate shift from concept shift.
